summary:
I've spent the last few weeks deep in a SillyTavern extension I'm calling character-forge — a tool that turns a chat interview into a full character card: personality, backstory, world lore, even art. It builds in stages (interview, brief, build, lint) so a bad answer doesn't wreck the whole card, and I've been shipping it in small versions almost daily as I hit real bugs. The nastiest one: a build step that ran on a device with no saved chat history would just invent a new character from scratch and silently overwrite the one that was already synced — cost me a character I had to hand-restore from a settings backup before I could fix the actual bug.

The art side has been its own project. Cards can now get an AI-generated portrait or scene image, pulled through whatever checkpoint is already configured for that source rather than a style system I made up — so it respects presets someone already tuned. Each image costs a GPU swap that takes 30-40 seconds round trip, since I'm running everything through a single shared GPU (a single Tesla P100) that has to unload and reload models depending on who's asking. I wrote the broker that manages that hand-off — a small proxy that decides which model gets the card and evicts whoever's not using it, with warm-start paths so it doesn't pay that cost on every request.

Most of the rest of my Claude time goes into BudgetTracker, a finance tracking app I run for myself that's grown into something closer to production software — Postgres behind Drizzle, Cloudflare Access in front, a set of read-only MCP tools so an agent can pull real numbers (account balances, spending trends) instead of guessing. The interesting failure mode there was in the data layer, not the UI: a few date-handling bugs in raw SQL that only showed up under specific query patterns, the kind of thing that passes review and breaks in production.

Underneath all of it is a home automation agent I built and keep tuning, mostly for myself — voice briefings, spending summaries, message routing across email and chat. The infrastructure work is unglamorous (systemd units, SSH keyrings, model routing) but it's taught me more about failure recovery than anything else I've built: what happens when a shared resource gets contended, when a process needs to survive a migration, when "it broke" turns out to be a stale cache three layers down instead of the thing everyone suspected first.

highlights.oneLiner: Broker serializing a single Tesla P100 across GPU consumers, GPU swaps in 30-40s
Personal finance app on Postgres/Drizzle behind Cloudflare Access; read-only MCP tools for agent queries
Home automation agent handling voice briefings, spending summaries, and message routing
